title: Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Theory of ODEs curriculum: existence and uniqueness theory (Picard-Lindelof, Lipschitz condition), linear systems and fundamental matrices, series solutions about ordinary and regular singular points (Frobenius method), Sturm-Liouville theory and boundary value problems, and qualitative/stability theory (phase plane, linearization, Lyapunov methods).

questions.question: The Picard-Lindelof existence and uniqueness theorem for y' = f(x,y), y(x0)=y0 requires f to be:
options: Continuous and Lipschitz continuous in y on a region containing (x0,y0)
questions.correct_answer: Continuous and Lipschitz continuous in y on a region containing (x0,y0)
questions.explanation: Continuity gives existence and the Lipschitz condition in y gives uniqueness of the solution near (x0,y0).

questions.question: A function f(x,y) satisfies a Lipschitz condition in y on a region D if there exists a constant L such that:
options: |f(x,y1) - f(x,y2)| <= L|y1 - y2| for all (x,y1),(x,y2) in D
f(x,y) <= L for all (x,y) in D
f is differentiable with f'(y) = L
questions.correct_answer: |f(x,y1) - f(x,y2)| <= L|y1 - y2| for all (x,y1),(x,y2) in D
questions.explanation: This is the defining inequality of a Lipschitz condition, bounding how fast f can change with y.

questions.question: The Picard iteration scheme for solving y' = f(x,y), y(x0)=y0 constructs successive approximations by:
options: y_(n+1)(x) = y0 + integral from x0 to x of f(t, y_n(t)) dt
questions.correct_answer: y_(n+1)(x) = y0 + integral from x0 to x of f(t, y_n(t)) dt
questions.explanation: Picard iteration converts the IVP into an integral equation and generates successive approximations by repeated integration.

questions.question: If df/dy is continuous and bounded on a rectangle containing (x0,y0), then f automatically satisfies:
options: Only continuity, never a Lipschitz condition
A Lipschitz condition in x instead
questions.explanation: By the Mean Value Theorem, a bounded continuous partial derivative in y implies f is Lipschitz in y with L equal to the bound.

questions.question: For a linear system X' = A(t)X where A(t) is an n by n matrix of continuous functions, a fundamental matrix Phi(t) is a matrix whose columns:
options: Form a set of n linearly independent solutions of the system
Sum to zero for all t
questions.correct_answer: Form a set of n linearly independent solutions of the system
questions.explanation: A fundamental matrix is built from n linearly independent solution vectors, and every solution is a linear combination of its columns.

questions.question: The Wronskian W(t) of n solutions of the linear system X' = A(t)X satisfies Abel's formula:
options: W(t) = W(t0) exp(integral from t0 to t of trace A(s) ds)
questions.correct_answer: W(t) = W(t0) exp(integral from t0 to t of trace A(s) ds)
questions.explanation: Abel's formula expresses the Wronskian's evolution in terms of the trace of the coefficient matrix.

questions.question: If the Wronskian of n solutions of a linear homogeneous system is nonzero at one point t0 in the interval of continuity of A(t), then:
options: It is nonzero for all t in that interval, and the solutions are linearly independent
It must be zero for all other t
The system then has no unique solution
questions.correct_answer: It is nonzero for all t in that interval, and the solutions are linearly independent
questions.explanation: By Abel's formula the Wronskian is either identically zero or never zero on the interval, so nonvanishing at one point implies linear independence throughout.

questions.question: A point x0 is called an ordinary point of the ODE y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0 if:
options: Both p(x) and q(x) are analytic at x0
p(x) has a pole at x0
questions.correct_answer: Both p(x) and q(x) are analytic at x0
questions.explanation: An ordinary point is one where the coefficient functions have convergent power series expansions, allowing a standard power series solution.

questions.question: A point x0 is a regular singular point of y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0 if p or q is singular there but:
options: (x - x0)p(x) and (x - x0)^2 q(x) are both analytic at x0
x0 is an ordinary point of q(x) only
questions.correct_answer: (x - x0)p(x) and (x - x0)^2 q(x) are both analytic at x0
questions.explanation: This is the standard test for a regular singular point, permitting a Frobenius-type series solution.

questions.question: The method used to find series solutions about a regular singular point is called:
questions.explanation: The Frobenius method generalizes power series solutions to allow a leading factor x^r, needed at regular singular points.

questions.question: In the Frobenius method, one seeks a solution of the form y = sum of a_n x^(n+r), where r is determined by:
questions.explanation: Substituting the trial series and collecting the lowest-order term gives the indicial equation, a quadratic in r.

questions.question: If the two roots r1, r2 (r1 > r2) of the indicial equation differ by a positive integer, the second Frobenius solution generally:
options: Is always a simple power series with no modification needed
questions.explanation: When roots differ by a positive integer, the recursion for the second solution can break down, requiring a log(x) term to complete the second independent solution.

questions.question: A Sturm-Liouville problem is a boundary value problem of the form:
options: d/dx[p(x) y'] + [q(x) + lambda w(x)] y = 0 with boundary conditions
y'' = lambda y only, with no boundary conditions
y' = lambda y with no boundary conditions
questions.correct_answer: d/dx[p(x) y'] + [q(x) + lambda w(x)] y = 0 with boundary conditions
questions.explanation: This self-adjoint form, together with separated boundary conditions, defines a regular Sturm-Liouville problem.

questions.question: For a regular Sturm-Liouville problem, eigenfunctions corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are:
options: Orthogonal with respect to the weight function w(x)
questions.correct_answer: Orthogonal with respect to the weight function w(x)
questions.explanation: This orthogonality follows from the self-adjointness of the Sturm-Liouville operator and underlies eigenfunction expansions.

questions.question: The eigenvalues of a regular Sturm-Liouville problem are:
options: Real, and can be ordered as an increasing sequence tending to infinity
questions.correct_answer: Real, and can be ordered as an increasing sequence tending to infinity
questions.explanation: Self-adjointness guarantees real eigenvalues, and regular Sturm-Liouville theory gives a discrete increasing sequence lambda_1 < lambda_2 < ... to infinity.

questions.question: An equilibrium point of an autonomous system X' = F(X) is a point X* such that:
options: X* is a solution passing through the origin only
questions.explanation: At an equilibrium point the vector field vanishes, so a solution starting there stays there for all time.

questions.question: Near an equilibrium point, the local behavior of a nonlinear autonomous system can often be approximated by studying:
options: The linearization given by the Jacobian matrix of F at the equilibrium
questions.correct_answer: The linearization given by the Jacobian matrix of F at the equilibrium
questions.explanation: The Hartman-Grobman theorem justifies using the linearized (Jacobian) system to describe local behavior near hyperbolic equilibria.

questions.question: If the Jacobian matrix at an equilibrium point has eigenvalues with strictly negative real parts, the equilibrium is classified as:
questions.explanation: Negative real parts of all eigenvalues mean nearby trajectories decay exponentially toward the equilibrium.

questions.question: If the Jacobian at an equilibrium of a 2D system has one positive and one negative real eigenvalue, the equilibrium is a:
questions.explanation: Mixed-sign real eigenvalues produce trajectories that approach along one eigendirection and depart along the other, the hallmark of a saddle.

questions.question: If the Jacobian eigenvalues at an equilibrium are purely imaginary and nonzero, the linearized system predicts a:
questions.explanation: Purely imaginary eigenvalues give closed elliptical trajectories around the equilibrium in the linear approximation.

questions.question: In Lyapunov's direct (second) method, if a function V(X) is positive definite near an equilibrium and its derivative along trajectories dV/dt is negative semi-definite, the equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: A Lyapunov function that is positive definite with non-increasing value along trajectories certifies stability without solving the system.

questions.question: A Lyapunov function V(X) used to prove asymptotic stability of an equilibrium at the origin must satisfy:
options: V(0)=0, V(X)>0 for X not equal to 0 near the origin, and dV/dt < 0 along trajectories near the origin
V(X) is negative for all X
questions.correct_answer: V(0)=0, V(X)>0 for X not equal to 0 near the origin, and dV/dt < 0 along trajectories near the origin
questions.explanation: These conditions ensure V acts as a strictly decreasing energy-like function, forcing trajectories to converge to the origin.

questions.question: The general solution of the linear system X' = AX, where A is a constant n by n matrix, can be written as:
questions.explanation: The matrix exponential e^(At) is the fundamental matrix solution of a constant-coefficient linear system, satisfying it directly.

questions.question: For a 2 by 2 constant matrix A with real distinct eigenvalues lambda1 and lambda2, both negative, the equilibrium at the origin of X'=AX is a:
questions.explanation: Two distinct negative real eigenvalues mean trajectories decay along both eigendirections, giving a stable node.

questions.question: The variation of parameters formula for the nonhomogeneous linear system X' = A(t)X + g(t), given a fundamental matrix Phi(t), gives the solution as:
options: X(t) = Phi(t)Phi(t0)^(-1)X0 + Phi(t) times the integral from t0 to t of Phi(s)^(-1) g(s) ds
questions.correct_answer: X(t) = Phi(t)Phi(t0)^(-1)X0 + Phi(t) times the integral from t0 to t of Phi(s)^(-1) g(s) ds
questions.explanation: This is the matrix analogue of the scalar variation of parameters formula, built from the fundamental matrix.

questions.question: The Legendre differential equation (1-x^2)y'' - 2xy' + n(n+1)y = 0 has x = 0 as:
options: A point where no solution exists
questions.explanation: The coefficient of y'' is nonzero and both coefficients are analytic at x = 0, so it is an ordinary point.

questions.question: The Legendre equation has regular singular points at:
questions.explanation: The leading coefficient (1-x^2) vanishes at x = 1 and x = -1, and both are regular singular points of the equation.

questions.question: Bessel's equation x^2 y'' + xy' + (x^2 - n^2)y = 0 has x = 0 as:
options: A point where the equation is undefined
questions.explanation: Dividing through shows p(x) and q(x) are singular at x=0 but xp(x) and x^2 q(x) remain analytic there, satisfying the regular singular point test.

questions.question: For Bessel's equation, the indicial equation gives roots r = plus or minus n. When 2n is not an integer, the two independent solutions are:
questions.explanation: When 2n is not an integer, both Frobenius series J_n and J_(-n) converge and are linearly independent.

questions.question: A boundary value problem differs from an initial value problem in that its auxiliary conditions are specified:
options: At two (or more) different points of the independent variable
questions.correct_answer: At two (or more) different points of the independent variable
questions.explanation: BVPs impose conditions at distinct points, such as the two endpoints of an interval, unlike IVPs which specify everything at one point.

questions.question: A homogeneous Sturm-Liouville boundary value problem has a nontrivial solution only for certain special values of lambda, called:
questions.explanation: These special values, together with their corresponding nontrivial solutions (eigenfunctions), are the central objects of Sturm-Liouville theory.

questions.question: For the two-point BVP y'' + lambda y = 0, y(0)=0, y(L)=0, the eigenvalues are:
questions.explanation: Solving this classic Sturm-Liouville problem with sine solutions vanishing at both endpoints yields lambda_n = (n pi/L)^2.

questions.question: The general solution of a second-order linear homogeneous ODE with constant coefficients whose characteristic equation has complex conjugate roots alpha plus or minus i beta is:
options: y = e^(alpha x)(C1 cos(beta x) + C2 sin(beta x))
y = C1 e^(alpha x) + C2 e^(beta x)
y = C1 cos(alpha x) + C2 sin(beta x)
questions.correct_answer: y = e^(alpha x)(C1 cos(beta x) + C2 sin(beta x))
questions.explanation: Complex conjugate roots produce oscillatory solutions modulated by an exponential envelope determined by the real part alpha.

questions.question: If f(x,y) fails to satisfy a Lipschitz condition in y near (x0,y0), the IVP y'=f(x,y), y(x0)=y0 may:
options: Have more than one solution through (x0,y0)
Always have a unique solution regardless
questions.correct_answer: Have more than one solution through (x0,y0)
questions.explanation: A classic example is y' = y^(1/3), y(0)=0, which fails the Lipschitz condition at y=0 and has multiple solutions through the origin.

questions.question: An n-th order linear ODE can always be rewritten as a first-order system of:
questions.explanation: Introducing the function and its first n-1 derivatives as new variables converts an n-th order ODE into an equivalent first-order system in n unknowns.
